prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock and its development to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18, opening a new regime of precision measurement with quantum-controlled atoms

statement.case_for: After reading the opening ballots I move from my own first choice, circuit QED (B018), to the optical lattice clock (B061). It is the one candidate that nearly every member ranked, five of eight in the top three, and the support comes from members with very different backgrounds: an experimental AMO physicist (Kroll), an atomic theorist (Lindroth), a particle and astroparticle physicist (Pearce) and me. That breadth says more than raw vote counts. On the science, the magic-wavelength idea is a clean, original concept that turned many neutral atoms into a clock without the usual lattice light shift. Ye's group then showed that blackbody, lattice light, collisional and cavity-related effects can be controlled to about 10^-18. This is a quantum-controlled experiment in which every physical detail is understood, and it has been reproduced and cross-compared at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere. The discovery content is not only the application: it is a new regime of metrology that tests relativity at the millimetre scale and probes constants and dark-matter couplings. The two-person credit of Katori for the concept and first realisation and Ye for the precision frontier and many-body clock physics is compact and well supported by the supplied names.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the underlying frequency-comb technology was already honoured in 2005 and ion-clock control in 2012, so part of the story can be called incremental, an ever-better clock rather than a new phenomenon. There is also the question of how much credit belongs to other groups at SYRTE, PTB and NIST and to the Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom generation of experimentalists, and the SI redefinition of the second has not yet happened, which some would call slightly early. Finally, I should be candid that my own first choice, B018, was deliberately dropped partly because Wallraff is missing from its credited names and because it sits close to the 2025 circuit prize.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as a measurement instrument in the strict sense, with 10^-18 uncertainty enabling geodesy, constants tests and dark-matter searches, and says the clock is distinct from the earlier comb and ion-clock prizes.
responses.response: I agree, and I find the distinctness argument convincing: the new element is the magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, which trades the single-ion statistics limit for stability and then makes it possible to study many-body shifts and collisions. Where I would add a qualification is on Kroll's comment that the broader field is mature: the best clock uncertainty is still improving, so the citation should point at the demonstrated regime rather than at a fixed record number.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B061 first and stresses that it rests on precise atomic-structure calculations and extremely well-controlled systematics, and she notes that other groups (Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow) blur the boundary a little.
responses.response: As someone who thinks about every systematic shift, I share her reading that the strength is in how controlled the device is, and her point about boundary groups is fair. I would still maintain that the two-name credit is defensible, since the concept and first lattice clock (Katori) and the route to the lowest systematic floor (Ye) are the decisive steps. I would also pair her enthusiasm for Cirac-Zoller (her rank 2, my rank 2) as the best alternative, though I do not think we can fit both within three laureates.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B061 sixth, calling it clear and impactful but arguably slightly early because the SI second has not yet been redefined and the technology is still advancing; his first choice is Aharonov and Berry (B008).
responses.response: I take the timing point seriously but disagree with it: the prize rewards the discovery, not the redefinition, and multiple independent laboratories agree at the 10^-18 level, which is the stability criterion I care most about. On B008 I respect the foundational weight of geometric phases, but I see it as two separate discoveries bridged by a theme, and I would want a sharper single citation before ranking it above a well-defined experimental breakthrough. I would be glad to hear whether he sees a way to write a unified citation.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B061 seventh and notes that the comb underpinning the clocks was recognised in 2005 and that other groups (Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom, Yb clocks) reached similar accuracy, while ranking the topological insulators (B019) first.
responses.response: The overlap with 2005 is a real qualification, but the comb is a tool here, not the discovery: lattice clocks need magic-wavelength trapping, which is new physics of its own. The parallel work on Yb clocks actually supports reproducibility rather than weakening the credit. I accept that B019 is conceptually elegant and I defer to him and the condensed-matter members on it, but the unresolved credit around Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang makes me hesitant to place it ahead of a case with a cleaner attribution.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle graphene (B013) first as an original, widely reproduced discovery, and ranks B061 third, supporting the Katori-Ye pair as a major measurement invention.
responses.response: I ranked B013 fourth and agree it is a striking discovery, but it is outside my core expertise and, as she herself says, the origin of the superconductivity is still debated and the omitted first author is a credit issue. I would not oppose it as a strong alternative if the committee prefers a condensed-matter prize this year, but with eight members ranking B061 and only six ranking B013, I see B061 as the safer consensus candidate.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat the lattice clock as a distinct discovery rather than an extension of the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether Ye's role as the precision-demonstration leader, versus other groups (Lemonde, Lisdat, NIST, PTB), is sufficient to justify the two-person credit without a third name.
Whether a combined prize with B034 would be preferable, which the three-person limit prevents without dropping a name.
My reading of the early history of lattice-clock demonstrations is from memory and has not been independently checked.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work closely with superconducting-circuit groups, so I should recuse myself from any discussion of B018 (circuit QED) and would not vote for it as a preferred part. I have no specific personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or the other lattice-clock groups, to Cirac and Zoller, or to the remaining shortlisted candidates apparent from the provided profile.
